### Enforce Exact Optional Property Types

Source: https://github.com/microsoft/typeScript-website/blob/v2/packages/tsconfig-reference/copy/en/options/exactOptionalPropertyTypes.md

Shows how the exactOptionalPropertyTypes flag restricts assigning 'undefined' to an optional property. This prevents runtime inconsistencies where 'undefined' might be treated differently than a missing key.

```typescript
// @exactOptionalPropertyTypes
// @errors: 2322 2412
interface UserDefaults {
  colorThemeOverride?: "dark" | "light";
}
declare function getUserSettings(): UserDefaults;

const settings = getUserSettings();
settings.colorThemeOverride = "dark";
settings.colorThemeOverride = "light";

// But not:
settings.colorThemeOverride = undefined;
```

### Handle Optional Property Undefined Values

Source: https://github.com/microsoft/typeScript-website/blob/v2/packages/documentation/copy/en/handbook-v2/Object Types.md

Shows how to safely access optional properties that might be undefined, either by checking for undefined or by providing default values.

```typescript
function paintShape(opts: PaintOptions) {
  let xPos = opts.xPos === undefined ? 0 : opts.xPos;
  let yPos = opts.yPos === undefined ? 0 : opts.yPos;
}
```

### TypeScript: Optional Parameters and Properties with strictNullChecks

Source: https://github.com/microsoft/typeScript-website/blob/v2/packages/documentation/copy/en/reference/Advanced Types.md

Explains how 'strictNullChecks' affects optional parameters and properties in TypeScript. Optional parameters automatically become 'number | undefined', and optional properties also include 'undefined' in their type. The example demonstrates type errors when 'null' is assigned where 'undefined' is expected.

```typescript
// @errors: 2345
function f(x: number, y?: number) {
  return x + (y ?? 0);
}

f(1, 2);
f(1);
f(1, undefined);
f(1, null);
```

```typescript
// @strict: false
// @strictNullChecks: true
// @errors: 2322
class C {
  a: number;
  b?: number;
}

let c = new C();

c.a = 12;
c.a = undefined;
c.b = 13;
c.b = undefined;
c.b = null;
```

### TypeScript 4.4 > Exact Optional Property Types

Source: https://github.com/microsoft/typeScript-website/blob/v2/packages/documentation/copy/en/release-notes/TypeScript 4.4.md

By default, TypeScript treats optional properties as if they include 'undefined' in their type, meaning a missing property and a property explicitly set to 'undefined' are considered equivalent. This behavior can cause issues with JavaScript features like 'Object.assign', object spread, and 'for-in' loops, which behave differently based on whether a property actually exists. The 'exactOptionalPropertyTypes' flag in TypeScript 4.4 allows developers to enforce that optional properties are interpreted exactly as written, preventing the implicit addition of 'undefined' to the type. This flag is not part of the 'strict' family and requires 'strictNullChecks' to be enabled.

--------------------------------

### Exact Optional Property Types

Source: https://github.com/microsoft/typeScript-website/blob/v2/packages/tsconfig-reference/copy/en/options/exactOptionalPropertyTypes.md

With `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` enabled, TypeScript applies stricter rules around how it handles properties on `type` or `interfaces` which have a `?` prefix. For example, this interface declares that there is a property which can be one of two strings: 'dark' or 'light' or it should not be in the object. Without this flag enabled, there are three values which you can set `colorThemeOverride` to be: "dark", "light" and `undefined`. Setting the value to `undefined` will allow most JavaScript runtime checks for the existence to fail, which is effectively falsy. However, this isn't quite accurate; `colorThemeOverride: undefined` is not the same as `colorThemeOverride` not being defined. For example, `"colorThemeOverride" in settings` would have different behavior with `undefined` as the key compared to not being defined. `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` makes TypeScript truly enforce the definition provided as an optional property.
